# HyperFund / HyperVerse: Investigation of the Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive assessment

The evidence supports a coherent, alleged recruitment-and-payment architecture in which HyperFund was promoted as a cryptocurrency and decentralized-finance opportunity, offered unusually high “passive” returns, relied on multi-level referral incentives, and later rebranded as HyperVerse and HyperNation when investor confidence and withdrawals deteriorated. The alleged business model combined four mutually reinforcing elements:

1. **Ponzi-like payment mechanics:** promised daily returns were allegedly funded primarily by new investor deposits rather than legitimate mining or operating revenue.
2. **Pyramid-style recruitment:** existing participants could earn additional rewards by recruiting investors through downlines extending to multiple levels.
3. **Public credibility-building:** promoters, online presentations, founder biographies, celebrity videos, and purported business affiliations were used to reduce perceived risk.
4. **Rebranding and narrative substitution:** HyperFund was reintroduced as HyperVerse and later HyperNation, changing the project’s story from decentralized finance to a metaverse and then a blockchain-based society.

The SEC complaint provides the most detailed account, but its factual assertions are allegations in a civil pleading rather than final judicial findings. Brenda Chunga pleaded guilty to a federal conspiracy charge, while the DOJ page reports that Rodney Burton was sentenced in July 2026. Sam Lee remained described as a defendant in the materials supplied. Accordingly, this report distinguishes allegations, established procedural events, and analytical assessments. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

The principal sources are:

- **S1:** CNBC’s January 29, 2024 report summarizing DOJ criminal charges and the related SEC action.
- **S2:** The SEC’s January 29, 2024 civil complaint against Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Chunga.
- **S3:** The DOJ’s HyperFund case page, including case numbers, procedural developments, and the government’s summary of the alleged scheme.
- **S4:** The Guardian’s January 2024 investigation concerning the purported HyperVerse chief executive “Steven Reece Lewis.”

The SEC complaint and DOJ case page are the strongest sources for legal allegations and procedural events because they are primary government records. CNBC is useful as contemporaneous reporting on the announcement. The Guardian is particularly relevant to the identity and biography of “Steven Reece Lewis,” although its findings should be understood as journalistic investigation rather than adjudicated fact.

## The alleged operating model

### Memberships and promised returns

According to the SEC complaint, HyperFund launched in June 2020 and sold “membership” packages using Tether, or USDT. The packages were represented internally through “HyperUnits,” with examples including $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000 membership levels. Promoters allegedly told investors that memberships provided access to educational content and future cryptocurrency offerings, but the central inducement was a daily reward of approximately 0.5% to 1% until the investor had received as much as three times the initial investment. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC alleged that these memberships were investment contracts because investors contributed money to a common enterprise and expected profits from the efforts of HyperFund, its operators, and their agents. The complaint further alleged that the memberships were securities offered without SEC registration or a valid exemption. These are legal allegations asserted by the SEC, not a final judicial determination in the supplied record. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The promised rate was economically extraordinary. A nominal return of 0.5% per day, if continuously compounded, would be inconsistent with ordinary investment returns; the promotional structure instead capped the advertised reward at a multiple of the initial investment. The central investigative significance is not merely the size of the promised return, but the way it was presented as relatively passive and systematic. Chunga allegedly told prospective investors that their initial investment could be recovered in roughly seven months and that subsequent payments would represent “pure profit.” ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Alleged Ponzi mechanics

The SEC alleged that HyperFund had no meaningful revenue source apart from money received from investors and that withdrawals were funded by later deposits. It specifically alleged that HyperFund did not operate the large-scale cryptocurrency-mining business used to justify the promised rewards. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ’s description is similar: promoters allegedly claimed that returns would be paid from cryptocurrency-mining operations that did not exist. DOJ described the alleged scheme as a worldwide $1.89 billion cryptocurrency fraud scheme, while CNBC reported the figure as approximately $1.9 billion. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The SEC complaint also alleges that Lee acknowledged in a 2023 call that the relevant group had exited bitcoin mining in 2019 and no longer owned mining machines. The complaint further alleges that he knew promotional materials continued to describe extensive mining operations. Because these assertions appear in the SEC’s complaint, they should be treated as allegations attributed to the SEC, even though the complaint quotes the alleged call in detail. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Recruitment and downline incentives

HyperFund allegedly did not rely only on passive-return promises. It also offered “accelerated” or leveraged rewards for recruitment. The SEC described three categories:

| Incentive | Alleged mechanism |
|---|---|
| Community Rewards | Compensation based on referred investors and their downlines, allegedly extending to 20 levels |
| VIP Rewards | Additional rewards tied to specified team or membership-sales thresholds |
| Global Rewards | A pool allegedly funded by a percentage of company sales and distributed to top promoters |

([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This structure created a powerful distribution mechanism. An investor could be presented with two paths to income: waiting for daily rewards or recruiting others to accelerate earnings. The distinction matters because recruitment both generated new deposits and transformed investors into salespeople. The SEC alleged that promoters encouraged “rebuys,” meaning reinvestment of rewards rather than withdrawal, which could keep funds inside the system and create the appearance of account growth without corresponding liquidity. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The Guardian similarly reported that members were paid in HyperUnits for recruiting new members, with commissions extending through as many as 20 levels. It also reported that the minimum membership was $300 and that the advertised reward structure promised a 300% return over 600 days. ([S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## Public promoters and credibility engineering

### Brenda Chunga’s alleged role

The SEC characterized Brenda Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” as one of HyperFund’s leading promoters and a major figure in its U.S. promotional presence. The complaint alleged that she joined in September 2020, began hosting online presentations, became one of only six corporate presenters, and reached the highest “VIP 5 STAR” level within approximately six months. That level allegedly required at least $5 million in referred membership sales. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC alleged that Chunga received approximately $3.7 million, composed of roughly $2.5 million withdrawn through the platform and approximately $1.1 million obtained directly from investors. The complaint states that she used funds for personal expenditures including luxury goods, vehicles, real estate, and a recruitment-related birthday event. These financial figures and expenditure descriptions are SEC allegations. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ page states that Chunga pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud. CNBC reported the same event and noted that she separately agreed to settle related SEC charges, including disgorgement and civil penalties to be determined later. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

### Rodney Burton and the broader promoter network

Rodney Burton, known as “Bitcoin Rodney,” was charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money-transmitting business and operating such a business. The DOJ page reports that Burton was sentenced on July 23, 2026, to 32 months’ imprisonment, with credit for time served, followed by three years of supervised release. ([S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The supplied materials do not establish that every promoter knew the alleged underlying business was fraudulent. They do, however, describe an organized promotional environment involving online seminars, presentations, referral links, downlines, and status-based rewards. The most defensible assessment is that public promoters were not incidental participants: they were central to the scheme’s alleged customer-acquisition strategy.

## Rebranding as a continuity mechanism

### HyperFund to HyperVerse

The SEC alleged that HyperFund rebranded as HyperVerse around December 2021. The new narrative emphasized a virtual world, avatars, a metaverse ecosystem, and a proposed native token called HVT. Mechanically, however, existing investors were allegedly transferred into the new platform, while the reward structure remained similar: 0.5% daily returns up to three times the initial investment over 600 days. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This combination of a new story and continuing economic promises is significant. The rebrand may be assessed as a method of preserving continuity while changing the product narrative. Investors could be encouraged to interpret operational problems as technological or developmental issues associated with launching a new platform rather than as evidence of insolvency. The SEC alleged that withdrawal problems began during the transition, became severe by February or March 2022, and were explained by promoters as platform or technology problems. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### HyperVerse to HyperNation

The SEC alleged that HyperVerse was rebranded again as HyperNation in approximately May 2022. HyperNation introduced a political and ideological narrative involving a decentralized government, inequality, injustice, and blockchain-enabled autonomy. Membership packages were relabeled as NFTs, and investors allegedly had to surrender or convert previously earned rewards to participate in the new structure. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The Guardian reported that HyperNation used masked figures called “Mr H” and “Miss N,” who were presented as ambassadors. It also reported that a promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity” within the same setup. The latter is evidence of a promoter’s statement, not independent proof of corporate structure. ([S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## The questionable CEO persona

### “Steven Reece Lewis”

The HyperVerse launch presented a person named “Steven Reece Lewis” as chief executive. Promotional materials allegedly described him as a University of Leeds graduate with a master’s degree from Cambridge, a former Goldman Sachs employee, the seller of a web-development company to Adobe, and the founder of an information-technology startup. ([S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The Guardian reported that it could not verify those credentials: neither university reportedly had a record under that name; no relevant Companies House or SEC record was found; Adobe filings did not show the claimed acquisition; and Goldman Sachs reportedly found no employment record. The Guardian also reported that the online presence associated with the name was limited and short-lived. ([S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The SEC complaint goes further, alleging that “Steven Reece Lewis” was a fabricated character portrayed by a paid actor who worked as a television presenter in Thailand. The complaint also alleges that Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the person was not the actual CEO. These statements remain allegations in the civil complaint. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Celebrity endorsements

The Guardian reported that HyperVerse released videos featuring Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The videos allegedly encouraged support for HyperVerse but did not mention investments or money. The Guardian expressly reported that there was no suggestion the celebrities understood the alleged business model when recording the messages. ([S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This distinction is important. The evidence supports the use of celebrity-facing promotional content as a credibility signal, but it does not support attributing knowledge of fraud to those individuals.

## Collapse, withdrawal restrictions, and scale

The sources differ on the precise date when withdrawals became blocked. CNBC and DOJ summarize the allegation as beginning in at least July 2021. The SEC complaint states that investors experienced difficulty during late 2021, could not withdraw by February or March 2022, and were unable to redeem investments by November 2022 after the HOO Exchange stopped functioning. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The amount allegedly raised also varies. DOJ identifies approximately $1.89 billion, CNBC rounds the figure to $1.9 billion, while the SEC alleges more than $1.7 billion. The Guardian cited a Chainalysis estimate of approximately $1.3 billion in consumer losses during 2022, which is a different measure from total funds raised. These figures should not be treated as interchangeable. ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## Overall conclusion

The strongest evidence-based conclusion is that HyperFund/HyperVerse allegedly operated as a recruitment-driven crypto investment network whose marketing, reward design, and rebranding were mutually reinforcing. High daily returns attracted initial investors; referral commissions converted them into promoters; claims of mining, corporate expertise, and celebrity support supplied legitimacy; and successive rebrands offered a new narrative when the prior platform experienced withdrawal problems.

The “Steven Reece Lewis” episode appears especially significant because it allegedly supplied a new executive identity at the moment HyperFund was being repositioned as HyperVerse. The SEC’s allegation that the persona was an actor, together with the Guardian’s inability to verify the stated biography, materially undermines the credibility architecture described in the promotional materials. Nevertheless, the criminal and civil allegations must be separated from final adjudicated findings. Chunga’s guilty plea and Burton’s reported sentence are procedural outcomes concerning those defendants; they do not, by themselves, establish every factual allegation against Lee or every allegation in the SEC complaint.

## References

CNBC. (2024, January 29). *DOJ and SEC unveil charges in $1.9 billion HyperFund cryptocurrency fraud*. [https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html) [S1]

Securities and Exchange Commission. (2024, January 29). *Complaint: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga, Civil Action No. 24-cv-00296*. [https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11) [S2]

United States Department of Justice. (2026, July 29). *HyperFund and associated cases*. [https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases) [S3]

Martin, S. (2024, January 4). *Chief executive of collapsed crypto fund HyperVerse does not appear to exist*. The Guardian. [https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist) [S4]

**Clarifying conflicting details**

I'm noting some contradictions in figures, like the amounts 1.9 versus 1.7 or 1.89. There's also a discrepancy in withdrawal dates, which range from July 2021 to February or March 2022. The DOJ page states things are pending, but there's a sentencing for Burton mentioned as well. Good to remember that I need to make sure my JSON is properly formatted after the report. No markdown links, but strings are fine.
